text:
Africa does not begin its infrastructure-finance problem with an empty savings account.

Our research examines the harder question: how domestic savings become assets that pension funds, insurers and other long-term investors can prudently buy.

A road, power system, warehouse or data network usually earns revenue in local currency. Financing it with dollar or euro debt can create a serious mismatch. A project can keep serving the same customers and still become financially distressed because the currency moves.

At the same time, African financial institutions already hold substantial capital. OECD estimates cited in the paper put pension and insurance assets at roughly US$775 billion. A broader Africa Finance Corporation estimate puts pension and insurance funds, public development banks and sovereign wealth funds above US$1.1 trillion.

Those figures do not mean there is a trillion-dollar pot waiting to be “unlocked”.

Trustees are supposed to be cautious. Government bonds are familiar, liquid and easy to value. Infrastructure projects often bring construction risk, uncertain tariffs, long tenors and limited secondary markets.

So the policy challenge is not simply to raise investment limits. It is to make projects genuinely investable.

StoneComms proposes a Local Capital Conversion Chain: turn savings into investable pools; projects into dependable cash-flow assets; concentrated risks into acceptable credit through preparation and guarantees; and individual deals into a market that can price, refinance and repeat them.

Recent guarantee and local-currency facilities in Nigeria, East Africa and West Africa show what that machinery can look like.

The central point is straightforward: domestic capital will not replace good project preparation. It rewards it.

Which part of the chain is the biggest constraint today: project preparation, credit enhancement, local-currency tenor, or secondary-market liquidity?
